title: Central Limit Theorem Simulator
summary: One picture with two panels on a shared value axis keeps the three objects apart: the population above, the most recent sample drawn as ticks along its axis, and beneath them the pile of sample means. Four populations are offered - normal, strongly right-skewed, uniform and bimodal - each with exactly known mean, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis, so the tool can print what theory predicts for the sample mean beside what the simulation produced, row by row. Because the predicted skewness of the mean is the population's divided by the square root of n, the familiar advice that thirty is enough becomes something a student can check and, for the skewed population, disprove.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a population, a sample and a sampling distribution.
Describe the sample mean as a random variable with its own distribution.
State where the sampling distribution is centred and why the standard error is the population SD over the square root of n.
Explain why the data do not become more normal as the sample grows.
Judge how fast convergence happens from the population's own skewness and kurtosis rather than from a rule of thumb.
interactionTypes: two-panel chart on a shared axis
theory beside simulation, row by row
shared or zoomed scale for the means
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every sample is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, a number input, radio groups, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the sample-size slider announces 'samples of 25 observations each'. The two-panel chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired inside its figure with a visible four-row table giving the predicted and simulated centre, standard deviation, skewness and excess kurtosis of the sample mean, and a disclosure holds the exact properties of the population currently selected. Each panel is labelled in words inside the picture, the panels are divided by a rule, the population mean is a dashed labelled line, and the axis note states whether the two panels share a scale, so nothing depends on colour or position alone. The pinned primary result measures 571px tall at 1366x768. Every draw, population change and scale change announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to the simulator heading when it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: The population, one sample and the sampling distribution, kept visibly apart
simulationNotes: Four populations are used, each a mathematical distribution with exactly known moments so that the predicted column of the table is not itself an estimate: Normal(50, 12); a shifted exponential, 20 plus an exponential of mean 20, giving mean 40, SD 20, skewness 2 and excess kurtosis 6; Uniform(20, 80), giving SD 17.32 and excess kurtosis -1.2; and an equal mixture of Normal(30, 6) and Normal(70, 6), whose central moments give SD 20.88 and excess kurtosis -1.683. For a mean of n independent draws the theory predicts centre mu, standard deviation sigma over the square root of n, skewness equal to the population's divided by the square root of n, and excess kurtosis equal to the population's divided by n; all four are shown beside the values measured from the simulated means. The simulated skewness and kurtosis use the ordinary sample formulae, which are biased downwards, and the tool says so on screen once a thousand means have been drawn. Changing the population or the sample size clears the pile, because those means came from a different sampling distribution. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32, using Box-Muller normals and inverse-CDF exponentials. Nothing on the page is real data, and the simulation does not prove the theorem - it agrees with it, and both rest on the same assumptions.
